source: Shah, Smith and Vargas-Hernandez (2003) Metrics for measuring ideation effectiveness (Design Studies 24(2):111-134), novelty section
finding: Founding paper opened in full text. Novelty of one idea is M1 = sum over functions j and stages k of f_j * S1_jk * p_k (f_j weights by function importance, p_k by stage importance). S1 comes two ways: (a priori) an expert-built scale of solution types, or (a posteriori) S1 = (T - C)/T * 10, where T is the number of ideas produced for that function and C is how many used the same solution. So novelty is relative to a reference universe (a priori) or to the set itself (a posteriori).
numbers: Worked example: 46 aircraft-like entries, four attributes with weights thrust 0.35, medium of travel 0.35, motion 0.20, number of pieces 0.10. The a priori scale used only three values (3, 7, 10). Entry 1 scored 3.00 (a priori) and 3.28 (a posteriori); entry 19 scored 8.05 (a priori). Correlation a priori vs a posteriori = 0.944. Correlation of each with peer evaluation = 0.624 (a posteriori) and 0.591 (a priori).
limits: Peer raters were the competing students, not an expert panel (the authors say so). One worked example and no inter-rater statistic for the a priori scale. The a posteriori score changes whenever ideas are added to the set.
agent_relevance: The cheap novelty score is a frequency count: (T-C)/T*10 per attribute. An agent can compute it on its own candidate set with no judge model, but it only means 'rare inside this set', not 'new to the world'.

source: Shah, Smith and Vargas-Hernandez (2003) Metrics for measuring ideation effectiveness, variety section (genealogy tree)
finding: Confirms the level weights 10/6/3/1 from the paper itself (gap 1 closed for the formulas). Ideas are sorted into a genealogy tree per function: level 1 physical principle (10), level 2 working principle (6), level 3 embodiment (3), level 4 detail (1). Variety M3 = sum_j f_j sum_k S_k * b_k / n, with b_k the number of branches at level k and n the number of ideas (the maximum is 10 per idea). A level with only one branch scores zero. The authors say the weights were 'assigned' so that a split at a higher level always outweighs splits below. Levels can be dropped when ideas lack detail.
numbers: Fig. 4 example: n = 11 ideas, one function, branches 2/5/6/4 at the four levels: M3 = (2*10 + 5*6 + 6*3 + 4*1)/11 = 72/11 = 6.54. Table 6-7 example with two functions (weights 0.6 and 0.4), two sets of 6 ideas: low-variety set M3 = 2.6, high-variety set M3 = 8.7.
limits: Weights are a design choice, with no empirical fit or sensitivity test in the paper. Placing ideas into levels is a human judgement and the paper gives no inter-rater number for it; I found no reliability coefficient for variety by keyword search of the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Variety is a count of branches in a tree, weighted by depth. The depth idea (principle > working principle > embodiment > detail) is the part worth keeping: an agent could ask an LLM to tag each idea with a physical principle and count distinct tags.

source: Shah, Smith and Vargas-Hernandez (2003) Metrics for measuring ideation effectiveness, quality, quantity and closure
finding: Quality is a separate task-specific score M2 = sum f_j S_jk p_k / sum f_j on a scale of 10, so it needs a spec-based evaluation. Quantity is the raw count of ideas submitted; the authors count every idea separately because variety already captures how different they are. They justify quantity by the common belief that more ideas raise the chance of a better one, and by fluency being used as a creativity score in psychology. Variety is there to stop quantity being inflated by trivial variants. The closing says no comprehensive model of design creativity exists yet.
numbers: No pooled effect size in this paper: it gives procedures and worked cases, not a validation study. The 2000 method-comparison paper (Shah, Kulkarni, Vargas-Hernandez, J Mech Design) could not be opened this session (search budget ran out, publisher page paywalled), so its numbers stay unknown.
limits: The quantity-to-quality link is stated as belief with citations, not shown here. The four metrics were designed for human sessions, not for sampling from a model.
agent_relevance: Keep the four measures separate in the agent log: count, spread (variety), rarity (novelty), fit to spec (quality). Do not merge them into one score.

source: Heuresis (2026) Search Strategies for Autonomous AI Research Agents Across Quality, Diversity and Novelty (arXiv 2606.25198)
finding: Six search strategies (greedy, MAP-Elites, Go-Explore, Islands, Curiosity, Omni) ran on three ML research tasks with Gemini-3.1-Pro agents. Every idea was executed and scored for quality, embedding diversity and literature-grounded novelty (5-point scale of Gupta and Pruthi, rated by a Claude Sonnet 4.6 agent with web search). Diversity-forcing archives (MAP-Elites, Go-Explore) top the diversity ranking on every task, but diversity did not predict quality or novelty, and novel ideas never reached the quality peak.
numbers: 3,222 scored runs. No idea rated 'Original' (NS=1). Largest share of NS=2 ideas on any task: 14.1% (Omni, Model Unlearning); Curiosity had 20 of 200 nanoGPT runs at NS=2, other strategies 0. Only 1 idea in the top-10 by quality is also NS<=2. Best novel-side vs best overall: nanoGPT val_bpb 0.9873 vs 0.9567 (3.2% gap); Unlearning 0.9689 vs 1.0309 (6.0%); median quality of NS<=2 ideas matches NS>=4 within 2.4%. Greedy had the lowest median pairwise distance (0.088 nanoGPT, 0.118 Unlearning). Running-best flattens after 50-100 valid solutions. 40 confirmed reward-hacking fabrications in 1,628 scored runs.
limits: One agent family and three ML tasks. The novelty rater is itself an LLM agent with search. No best-of-N sampling control arm. Executed outcomes are first-attempt only.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gaps 3 and 4: forced-divergence search raises spread, but spread did not convert to quality or novelty once ideas were executed. Log spread, but do not use it as the success signal.

source: Budgeted Subset Refinement (2026) allocating refinement effort over a pool of LLM research ideas (arXiv 2607.14118)
finding: On a shared pool of generated ideas, raw generation and reranking alone gave zero research-strong non-duplicate ideas. Refining every candidate worked but cost most and produced the most duplicates. Refining only 4 chosen candidates gave similar or better yield at lower token cost, and choosing them by maximal marginal relevance (diversity-aware) was best on a proxy rubric.
numbers: Table 1 (10 seeds x 10 environments; duplicate threshold cosine 0.82). Strong non-dup yield / cost per strong idea (tokens) / total tokens / duplicate rate: raw first-n 0.00 / - / 60.7k / 0.022; rerank only 0.00 / - / 77.4k / 0.072; refine all 21.80 / 5387 / 115.4k / 0.238; random-4 22.18 / 4859 / 105.0k / 0.186; MMR-4 23.70 / 4492 / 105.2k / 0.172. A blinded external judge on 72 items supported the refinement effect, but per-item rankings among refined methods changed with the judge.
limits: The rubric is a proxy scored by LLMs, not expert review or execution. MMR beats random-4 by about 1.5 ideas (about 7%); no confidence intervals read.
agent_relevance: Evidence on gaps 5 and 10: uniform refinement raised the duplicate rate from 0.022 (raw) to 0.238, so refinement concentrates ideas. Spend refinement on a diverse subset, not on every candidate.

source: Recoding-Decoding for sustained creativity and diversity in LLMs (2026, arXiv 2603.19519)
finding: A decoding wrapper that steers away from already-covered regions (a forced-divergence operator at token level) keeps producing new idea clusters over many runs, while ordinary decoding saturates early. Cluster counts agreed across ten clustering methods and relevance stayed near 0.99 (0.94 on DeepSeek-3).
numbers: Battlefield prompt: ordinary decoding gave 19 unique battlefields, recoding-decoding 1,307. Image-idea prompt: 250 ideas (50 runs x 5) gave 244 clusters with RD vs 35 with ordinary decoding. On 50 brainstorm topics x 50 runs, RD curves on the best model rise almost linearly (about 5 new clusters per run of 5), ordinary curves flatten. NoveltyBench subset: all 5 outputs distinct for 95.0% of prompts with RD vs 85.0% Verbalized Sampling, 82.0% human responses, 15.0% ordinary decoding. Cluster cosine thresholds 0.73 (brainstorm) and 0.83 (public datasets). LLM relevance judge: 80% majority agreement with humans on three levels, 97% after merging. Models: DeepSeek-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-5.1, Gemini-3.
limits: Single group. No equal-token or best-of-N comparison (RD adds editing passes). Diversity is embedding-cosine clusters, which the series already shows are threshold sensitive. Quality of the extra clusters was not tested beyond relevance.
agent_relevance: Gives the saturation curve for naive repeated sampling (35 clusters from 250 ideas) against a divergence operator (244). Partly answers gaps 3 and 10, but without the equal-token control gap 3 stays open.

source: Terwiesch, Meincke, Girotra, Mollick, Nave and Ulrich (2026) AI and Its Impact on Creativity and Diversity: An Empirical Study of LLM-Generated Product Ideas (arXiv 2607.27553), Study 3b
finding: Correction to K09. The 'refine twice' agent (Agent 1, 'Bold Ideas') ran on GPT-4o, the reference model of that study, so its 0.575 must be compared with GPT-4o zero-shot 0.679, not with the older GPT-4 0.585. Refining each idea twice to make it 'bolder' cut diversity by about 0.10; the authors say ideas converged on shared features (especially scents) like local search stuck on one peak. One-idea independent sessions were far worse than one session producing many ideas.
numbers: Diversity = 1 - mean pairwise cosine similarity (Universal Sentence Encoder): humans 0.773; random personas 0.757; agent 2 (human-picked problem, new solution) 0.739; random constraints 0.735; GPT-4o chain-of-thought 0.698; random sonnets 0.686; GPT-4o zero-shot 0.679; GPT-4 zero-shot 0.585; Agent 1 refine twice 0.575; GPT-4o independent single-idea sessions 0.452. 95% CIs about +-0.009.
limits: One product domain (cheap items for college students), one model (GPT-4o, Aug 2024) for the interventions, one embedding. Accepted July 2026 after two revisions. No equal-token control for the personas arm.
agent_relevance: Best direct number for gap 5: self-refinement toward 'bolder' lost 0.104 diversity on a 2024 model. For gap 3: independent resampling (best-of-N style, 0.452) is much more redundant than one session asked to avoid its own earlier ideas (0.679).

source: Terwiesch et al. (2026) AI and Its Impact on Creativity and Diversity, Study 3c (coverage versus number of LLM ideas) and the best-idea logic of Girotra et al. (2010)
finding: More LLM ideas steadily cover more of the human idea space, with no plateau by 1,000 ideas, but the hardest human ideas stay far away. The paper also restates Girotra et al. (2010): the quality of the best idea rises with (1) the number of ideas, (2) the average quality, (3) the variance of the idea distribution.
numbers: Coverage = cosine distance from each of 200 human ideas to its nearest LLM idea (GPT-4o, cumulative random subsets). Mean distance 0.546 at N=100 falls to 0.478 at N=1,000; maximum distance falls only from 0.762 to 0.711. Study 1a: GPT-4 ideas were 7x more likely than student ideas to be in the top 10% by purchase intent.
limits: One model and domain; N up to 1,000; random subsets, no selection step. Nearest-neighbour distance depends on the embedding. The fall from N=100 to 1,000 is only 0.068 in cosine distance.
agent_relevance: Gaps 9 and 10: for plain LLM sampling the saturation curve is slow and still falling at N=1,000. That favours 'sample wide then filter' only when generation is cheap; on a fixed token budget a divergence operator is the better lever.

source: Terwiesch et al. (2026) AI and Its Impact on Creativity and Diversity, E-Companion E (style standardization check)
finding: Tests whether the human-vs-LLM diversity gap is just a writing-style artefact of the embedding. All 400 ideas were rewritten into one neutral style by Claude Sonnet 4.5 and re-embedded. Most of the gap stayed.
numbers: Zero-shot gap B = 0.193 (95% CI 0.182-0.204) before and 0.154 (0.141-0.168) after standardization (80% retained); with word count as covariate 0.149. Few-shot gap 0.207 to 0.186 (90% retained), 0.177 with word count. 200 human, 100 GPT-4 zero-shot, 100 GPT-4 few-shot ideas.
limits: An LLM does the rewriting, which may smooth real differences. USE embedding only.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gaps 7 and 10: a style-neutralising rewrite before embedding is a cheap control, and here the gap survives it by 80-90%. Schaeffer's harder null shrank the headline much more.

source: Examining and Addressing Barriers to Diversity in LLM-Generated Ideas (2026, arXiv 2602.20408), Study 1 (human vs LLM, category-based diversity)
finding: GPT-4o (Nov 2024 snapshot) simulated 99 participants against 99 Prolific humans (121 recruited, 22 excluded for off-task time), each giving 10 fitness-product ideas. Diversity was scored by LLM-assigned categories on three dimensions (industry context, psychological need, product form), NOT by embeddings; the authors argue embeddings mismeasure because human wording varies and LLM wording is uniform. Human groups still cover more categories.
numbers: Whole sample: categories 28 (human) vs 22 (LLM) of max 28; unique combinations 206 vs 88 (990 ideas each). Bootstrapped groups of 10 people x 10 ideas: categories 26.29 vs 18.45; combinations 59.66 vs 39.15; mean pairwise distance 2.41 vs 2.04 (max 3.0), all p<.001. First ideas only: categories 14.51 vs 8.37, distance 2.41 vs 1.51.
limits: Categories were assigned by GPT-4o itself; no human check of the labels in the text I read. One product domain and a 2024 model.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a non-embedding diversity measure still shows the human advantage, so the gap is not only an embedding artefact. Most of the LLM loss is in the first idea of each session.

source: Examining and Addressing Barriers to Diversity in LLM-Generated Ideas (2026, arXiv 2602.20408), fixation and seeding (Studies 1-2)
finding: Within one session the LLM shows as much fixation as humans: its category count and accumulation slope over 10 sequential ideas match humans. Seeding an LLM session with a human first idea did not improve later diversity. This is a direct test of LLM fixation on an early output, though the 'example' is its own prior ideas or a seed idea, not a design exemplar as in Jansson and Smith.
numbers: Per person over 10 ideas: categories 12.68 (human) vs 12.46 (LLM), p=.45; combinations 8.37 vs 8.68, p=.12; pairwise distance 2.10 vs 2.11, p=.78. Accumulation slope 1.035 vs 1.013, p=.51 (max 3.0). Seeded vs default LLM (ideas 2-10): categories 18.35 vs 18.34 (p=.95), combinations 38.16 vs 38.22 (p=.89), distance 2.07 vs 2.07 (p=.49).
limits: GPT-4o only, one task. 'Fixation' is inferred from a slope below the theoretical maximum, which any set with repeated topics shows; there is no no-example control as in Jansson and Smith.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: first LLM-vs-human within-session fixation comparison opened; they are equal. It is not a replication of the Jansson-Smith example effect, so the design-exemplar test on LLMs is still open.

source: Examining and Addressing Barriers to Diversity in LLM-Generated Ideas (2026, arXiv 2602.20408), personas and chain-of-thought (Studies 3-4)
finding: Ordinary personas (varied backgrounds) closed the human-LLM gap and beat 'creative entrepreneur' personas, but increased within-session fixation. Chain-of-thought (draft ten short themes first, then write) reduced fixation in the LLM but not in humans. Persona plus CoT scored highest, above humans.
numbers: Unique combinations (990 ideas each): human 206, ordinary persona 210, creative entrepreneurs 164, default LLM 88. Between-participant variation of first ideas: ordinary persona 0.635, default LLM 0.241, human 0.545, creative entrepreneurs 0.429. CoT on default LLM: categories 18.45 to 24.84, combinations 39.15 to 55.49, distance 2.04 to 2.39 (all p<.001), slope 1.013 to 1.363. Persona + CoT: categories 24.02 to 26.51, combinations 56.97 to 65.42, slope 0.876 to 1.086. Human CoT: slope 1.035 to 1.035 (p=.997), categories 26.29 to 25.36.
limits: Single product domain, GPT-4o, bootstrapped groups of 10. The extra tokens for theme drafts are not equalised against simply drawing more samples.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a two-step operator (list distinct themes, then write one per theme) raised combinations by about 42% over default at the same idea count, but with more tokens, so the equal-token claim is still untested.

source: StructSim: Measuring Idea Similarity at Scale Through Structural Representation (2026, arXiv 2609.34046)
finding: Whole-text embeddings barely beat chance at picking which of two variants is structurally closer to a source idea, as judged by 12 engineers. A structure graph (purpose, mechanism, implementation) matched experts far better. The authors cite Shah's physical-principle and working-principle levels as the model for core versus detail differences.
numbers: Triple task, 233 triples where the expert majority picked one candidate: structure graph 0.871 accuracy; keyphrase-concat embedding (text-embedding-3-small) 0.562; whole-text text-embedding-3-small 0.524; keyphrase-concat MiniLM 0.524; whole-text all-MiniLM-L6-v2 0.511; BERTScore 0.481. Set coverage: graph-chosen ideas rated 3.37 vs 2.12 for embedding-chosen ideas (1-5 novelty against the existing corpus, Welch t = -5.11, p<.001); expert ICC(2,k) = 0.876. Four design problems, 100 initial ideas each, 12 experts (3 per problem).
limits: Triples were built to separate core mechanism from implementation, which is exactly where embeddings are weakest. Small expert group, one author team, method tuned by the authors.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to the missing validation for gaps 2 and 7: whole-text cosine is near chance (0.51-0.56) on mechanism-level 'same idea' calls. Do not use one-vector cosine as the divergence signal; tag the mechanism first.

source: Sankar and Sen (2025) Semantic characterization of ideation: a computational framework using vector embedding and clustering (J Eng Design; arXiv 2409.07578)
finding: Ideas were embedded with OpenAI text-embedding-3 (3072-d) and clustered with UMAP + DBSCAN. Thirty expert designers (5+ years) judged whether ideas A (same cluster), B (neighbouring cluster) and C (far cluster) were very similar, somewhat similar or very different from a reference idea. The dominant expert label matched cluster proximity for 10 of 12 reference ideas; in the 2 misses, 'very similar' and 'somewhat similar' were swapped but 'very different' still matched.
numbers: Six problem statements x 2 reference ideas = 12 comparisons; 30 experts; 100 ideas per problem from a conversational AI with an Action-Object-Context prompt. New metrics 'idea sparsity' and 'cluster sparsity' proposed.
limits: Coarse three-level comparison (same, near, far cluster). No genealogy-tree variety computed and no error rate for 'same idea' at a cosine cut. Contrast with StructSim: agreement holds for coarse topical distance and fails on mechanism-level contrasts.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: embeddings plus clustering agree with experts on coarse topic groups (10 of 12). No study opened compares them with Shah genealogy-tree variety, so the gap stays partly open.

source: Edwards, Tehranchi, Miller and Ahmed (2025) AI Judges in Design: statistical perspectives on achieving human expert equivalence with vision-language models (arXiv 2504.00938)
finding: Four VLM judges (in-context examples with or without reasoning, up to OpenAI o1) rated about 875 early concept sketches (934 in the set; milk-frother task) on uniqueness, creativity, usefulness and drawing quality. Expert equivalence was tested by weighted kappa, ICC, Bland-Altman, TOST and top-set Jaccard. The best judge (text + image examples + reasoning) reached expert-level agreement on uniqueness and drawing quality and matched or beat trained novices on all four.
numbers: Expert-expert kappa baselines: uniqueness 0.54, creativity 0.26, usefulness 0.59, drawing quality 0.33. Rule used: AI kappa and ICC at least 0.80 of the expert-expert value. The best judge met or exceeded the majority of trained novices in 6/6 runs for uniqueness and creativity and 5/6 for drawing quality and usefulness.
limits: Expert-expert kappa for creativity is only 0.26, so the bar there is low. One task and one rater pool, early-2025 models, sketches rather than text ideas.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a judge can reach expert-level agreement when it gets worked examples with expert scores and reasons before scoring. Zero-shot LLM novelty judging at 43-53% is not the ceiling. Calibrate the judge to a small human-rated panel.

source: Hirota et al. (2026) Aggregate vs. Personalized Judges in Business Idea Evaluation: Evidence from Expert Disagreement (arXiv 2604.22517), PBIG-DATA
finding: About 3,000 expert scores on 300 patent-grounded product ideas show weak agreement on exact scores but more agreement on which ideas are in the top half. LLM judges conditioned on the same evaluator's past scores aligned better than judges using pooled scores or a rubric only.
numbers: Krippendorff alpha for 'innovativeness' in three domains: 0.33 / 0.47 / 0.46; other dimensions often near zero or negative (technical validity -0.03, -0.40, -0.28). Coarse agreement (Jaccard of above-median sets) for innovativeness: 0.71 / 0.43 / 0.54. Personalized judges beat aggregate judges on 5 of 6 dimensions on Jaccard. Correlation between expert agreement and judge reasoning similarity r = 0.31 for personalized judges only. Qwen3 4B-235B plus GPT-5 mini in the appendix; predictions with confidence under 80 discarded.
limits: Business ideas from patents, not engineering design sessions. Experts disagree, so there is no single ground truth. Open-weight Qwen3 and GPT-5 mini only.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the human ceiling on fine-grained novelty scores is itself low (alpha 0.33-0.47). Use coarse selection (top half vs bottom half) and pairwise comparisons, not point scores.

source: Ashkinaze, Mendelsohn, Qiwei, Budak and Gilbert (2025) How AI Ideas Affect the Creativity, Diversity, and Evolution of Human Ideas (arXiv 2401.13481)
finding: Settles the record in K12/c22: the 0.31 for Ashkinaze is Cliff's delta, not beta. In a chain experiment (people see the latest earlier ideas, with or without AI ideas) on the Alternative Uses task, high AI exposure raised collective (global) diversity relative to the human-only control.
numbers: Global diversity = median pairwise cosine distance of sentence embeddings per condition. Cliff's delta vs control: high exposure disclosed 0.31 (p=0.001); high exposure undisclosed 0.26 (p=0.001). Over 3,000 responses from 48 countries. AI ideas from ChatGPT-3.5, zero-shot. Authors: 'AI made ideas different, not better'.
limits: Alternative Uses Task, ChatGPT-3.5, chain design where each person sees only the latest ideas. Differs from Doshi and Hauser (story writing, one GPT-4 prompt shown to all writers).
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a small-to-medium effect (delta 0.31) in the opposite direction from the 'AI homogenizes' papers. Task and exposure design matter: when each person sees different AI items, pooled diversity rises.

source: Wan and Kalman (2025) Diverse AI Personas Can Mitigate the Homogenization Effect in Human-AI Collaborative Ideation (arXiv 2504.13868)
finding: Extension of the Doshi and Hauser story task: ten AI personas generated 300 plots; participants saw 0, 1 or 5. Story diversity stayed at the human-only baseline. The authors argue the homogenization effect arises because everyone is shown the same AI output. Their own text describes the Doshi and Hauser result as cosine similarity rising by 10.7% and 8.9% (confirming the correction: that sentence is Wan and Kalman's wording).
numbers: Persona plot set vs single-prompt set: t = 119.94, Cohen's d = 1.4254. About 100 Prolific UK participants (earlier line b17 gives N=97, p=.57, power 55%).
limits: The 10.7/8.9% figure is from this paper's description, not from Doshi and Hauser's own text. Underpowered at 55%; Bayes factors ambiguous.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a likely cause of the conflict is source variety, not the model alone. One shared AI answer homogenizes; many varied answers do not.

source: Dong and Yakura (2026) Human diversity fuels collective creativity that large language models cannot simulate or sustain (arXiv 2607.26899)
finding: Preregistered creative-metaphor experiment with native and non-native English writers under three conditions: no AI, AI-generated ideas (ideation), or AI refining the writer's own idea (refinement). AI ideation compressed collective diversity for everyone; AI refinement preserved it. Simulated pools from three model families built from real participants' backgrounds all fell below every human pool.
numbers: Coefficients quoted in the text: b = 0.036 and b = 0.046 (both p<0.001) for the ideation-versus-other contrasts, and two AI conditions differing by b = 0.018 (p=0.12) in one comparison; I did not trace every contrast to its table. Independent evaluators N = 351; reliability rSB = 0.86 for divergent (novelty and surprise) and 0.87 for convergent items. Individual ratings rose with AI ideation.
limits: Metaphor task with English L1/L2 writers; preprint. Simulation scored by cosine to centroid. Contrasts above are quoted without a full table check.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 10: refining one's own seed idea keeps spread, while refining an LLM-made pool lost about 0.10 diversity (d07). The seed's source decides; self-critique of one's own output is the risky case.

source: Sio, Kotovsky and Cagan (2015) Fixation or inspiration? A meta-analytic review of the role of examples on design processes (Design Studies 39)
finding: Not opened (publisher abstract elided; page behind a redirect). Citing papers describe it as a meta-analysis of over 40 studies using the Jansson-Smith paradigm. Two citing papers give different headlines: one says examples lead to more concepts that copy the example; another says people produced fewer ideas with examples but those ideas were more novel, and quality tracked similarity to the example.
numbers: Study count 'over 40' only from citing-paper snippets; no effect sizes obtained.
limits: Second-hand through Semantic Scholar citation snippets. The two paraphrases conflict on idea count, so rely on neither.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the human baseline for the example effect is still unverified here. The meta-analysis exists; its pooled effects need someone with access to read it.

source: Nelson, Wilson, Rosen and Yen (2009) Refined metrics for measuring ideation effectiveness (Design Studies 30(6))
finding: Not opened (paywalled). Citing papers describe it as merging novelty and variety into one measure of design-space exploration while keeping quantity and quality, later reused as 'Nelson's criteria'.
numbers: No numbers obtained.
limits: Second-hand description only. Whether Nelson found a quantity-quality relation is unverified.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 (human side) stays open. Do not cite a Nelson quantity-quality coefficient.

source: Wadinambiarachchi et al. (2024) The Effects of Generative AI on Design Fixation and Divergent Thinking (arXiv 2403.11164), design and scope check
finding: Re-checked the design for K14. Humans (not LLMs) sketched chatbot avatars for 20 minutes after seeing an example avatar with 14 salient features, under three conditions: no support, Google image search, Midjourney V4. Fixation score = share of example features copied. So the study tests human fixation when helped by AI images; it does NOT test whether an LLM itself fixates on a provided example.
numbers: N = 60, between participants. Fixation, fluency, variety and originality scored from sketches. The abstract-level result read: the AI-image group showed higher fixation.
limits: One task, one image tool, student-type sample; I did not re-extract the group means.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: restate K14 as human fixation helped by AI images. The only LLM-self fixation data opened are d11 (GPT-4o sequential ideas), which equal humans.

source: Ma, Grandi, Ahmed et al. (2023) Conceptual Design Generation Using Large Language Models (arXiv 2306.01779), metrics check
finding: GPT-3 concepts for 12 design problems were compared with crowd concepts. Experts rated feasibility, novelty and usefulness (quality was dropped because earlier work showed the lowest inter-rater reliability for it). Computational metrics were SBERT cosine similarity and convex hull volume of the embedding set. Hull volume was lower for GPT-3 sets than for the crowd.
numbers: Mean hull volume: crowd 0.294 (SD 0.03); GPT-3 prompt variants 0.186-0.266 (the adjective-augmented prompt lowest at 0.186). Mean cosine similarity to the crowd set roughly 0.75-0.80. No Shah genealogy-tree variety was computed, and no correlation between the computed metrics and the expert ratings is reported in the text I read.
limits: GPT-3 (2023), prompt sensitive, text solutions only. The authors list metric validity as future work.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: confirms there is still no published check of embedding-set metrics against tree variety, even in a paper that used both metric families.

source: Gap search log: tools and coverage (this run)
finding: Not a source. WebSearch quota ran out partway through this run (shared 200-call limit), so I used arXiv HTML search, the Semantic Scholar citation graph and arXiv PDFs. Semantic Scholar listed 1,159 papers citing Shah et al. 2003. Among 2023-2026 LLM-related ones: StructSim, Sankar and Sen, Wadinambiarachchi, AI Judges in Design, Ma et al. (all opened), plus 'The Crowd Without People: Multi-agent LLMs as Idea Evaluators' (Group Decision and Negotiation 2026) and 'Exploring the use of LLMs to evaluate design creativity' (DS 2025), found but not opened.
numbers: 1,159 citing papers retrieved.
limits: Paywalled human studies (Sio 2015, Nelson 2009, Shah 2000, Girotra 2010, Linsey) could not be read.
agent_relevance: Next run: open the two unopened LLM-judge papers and obtain the Sio meta-analysis.
